title: The River, the Tree of Life, and Come, Lord Jesus
summary: The angel shows John the river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with the tree of life on either side, whose leaves are for the healing of the nations. There is no more curse, and God's servants will see his face. The book then closes with Jesus' repeated promise, “I am coming soon,” with invitations to the thirsty, warnings against changing the prophecy, and the church's answering prayer, “Come, Lord Jesus!”
story: This is the last page of the Bible, and it deliberately returns to the first. Genesis 2 opened with a garden, a river flowing out of Eden, and the tree of life; Genesis 3 ended with the curse, and with humanity driven out and cherubim guarding “the way to the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). Here the curse is gone, the tree stands open, and the river flows from God's own throne. In between lie the whole history of Israel, the coming of Jesus, his death and resurrection, and the mission of the church. The first five verses finish the vision of the city begun in 21:9. The rest of the chapter (verses 6-21) is the book's epilogue, which echoes its prologue in chapter 1 and turns from what John saw to how the churches should live while they wait.
historical:
The epilogue brings the reader back to the seven churches of Asia to whom the book was sent (1:4), and it assumes that the prophecy would be read aloud in their gatherings, as 1:3 says. Books were copied by hand, and copyists sometimes added or dropped words. Warnings against altering a text were a known feature of ancient writings, and the Old Testament had given one for the law, forbidding Israel to add to or take away from what God commanded (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). The warnings in verses 18 and 19 apply that concern to this book of prophecy. They were not written about the whole Bible as later collected, though many Christians have applied their principle more widely.

The prayer Come, Lord Jesus (verse 20) matches an Aramaic prayer of the earliest churches, maranatha, which Paul leaves untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22 (the BSB renders it “Come, O Lord!”). Its use in Greek-speaking churches suggests how early and how widely believers prayed for Christ's return. The early Christian manual known as the Didache, probably from around the late first or early second century, includes the same Aramaic word in its prayers after the Lord's Supper.
cultural:
Water was life in the dry lands of the Bible, and a river flowing from the temple was an old prophetic picture. Ezekiel saw a river flowing from the temple that made the Dead Sea fresh, with trees on both banks whose “fruit will be used for food and their leaves for healing” (Ezekiel 47:12). Zechariah saw living water flowing out from Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:8), and Psalm 46:4 speaks of a river whose streams make glad the city of God. John joins these pictures with Genesis: Ezekiel's many trees become the one tree of life, bearing fruit every month, and its leaves heal not Israel only but the nations.

Seeing God's face was the deepest longing of Israel's worship and also something no one could do and live; God told Moses that no one could see his face and survive (Exodus 33:20). The promise that “They will see His face” (verse 4) means that the barrier between a holy God and his people is gone. Dogs (verse 15) was a common insult in the ancient world for those considered impure or shameless, and here it stands with the other vices for those who remain outside by their own choice. The title “the bright Morning Star” (verse 16) refers to the planet Venus, which appears before dawn and announces the day; Numbers 24:17 had spoken of a star coming forth from Jacob.
literary: Verses 1-5 complete the vision of the city with the imagery of a restored Eden, so that the Bible ends with a garden inside a city. The epilogue that follows is less a narrative than a collage of voices: the angel, Jesus, John, the Spirit and the bride, and the hearer are all heard, sometimes without clear markers of who is speaking. Three times Jesus says he is coming soon (verses 7, 12, 20). Two beatitudes (verses 7 and 14) bring the book's total to seven. Many phrases repeat the prologue: “what must soon take place” (verse 6, compare 1:1), “the time is near” (verse 10, compare 1:3), the Alpha and the Omega (verse 13, compare 1:8), and the angel sent to show God's servants. The book closes, like a letter, with a grace: “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints” (verse 21).

outline.t: The river of the water of life and the tree of life
No more curse: they will see his face and reign forever
These words are faithful and true: John and the angel
Do not seal the book: I am coming soon, with my reward
Jesus' testimony and the invitation: Come
A warning not to add to or take from the prophecy
Come, Lord Jesus, and the closing blessing

doctrines.note: The Bible ends where it began, in a garden with the tree of life, but now within a city filled with the glory of God. God's purpose for creation, lost through sin, is not abandoned but completed and surpassed.

The curse of Genesis 3 is lifted, the way to the tree of life is open to those who have washed their robes (verse 14), and the water of life is offered freely to anyone who is thirsty (verse 17). Salvation is God's gift, received rather than earned.
The church waits for a person, not only for an event. The book's last promise is Jesus' own word that he is coming, and its last prayer is the church's reply.
The prophecy is called faithful and true, is not to be sealed, and must not be altered. It is given so that it can be heard, kept, and lived by the churches while they wait.

words.note: Xulon, wood or tree. The same word is used in the Greek Old Testament for the tree of life in Genesis 2-3. Elsewhere in the New Testament it is used several times for the cross (Acts 5:30; 1 Peter 2:24), which has led many readers to see a connection, though Revelation itself does not draw it. Here it names the tree that bears fruit every month and whose leaves heal the nations.

Zoe, life. Revelation uses it for the water of life, the tree of life, and the Book of Life. It means not bare existence but the life that belongs to God and that he shares, the life humanity lost access to in Genesis 3 and receives again here.

Katanathema, a curse, a thing under a ban. Verse 3 says there will no longer be any curse. The clear background is Genesis 3:17, where the ground was cursed because of Adam; the promise reverses that sentence and the whole history of death and frustration that came from it.

Erchomai, to come. It rings through the chapter: “Behold, I am coming soon” (verses 7 and 12), “Yes, I am coming soon” (verse 20), and the Spirit, the bride, and the hearer all say “Come” (verse 17). The same verb carries Christ's promise and the church's invitation to the thirsty.

christ: The Bible's last chapter is full of Christ. The river flows from “the throne of God and of the Lamb” (verse 1), one throne shared by God and the Lamb. Jesus calls himself “the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End” (verse 13), titles God gives himself in 1:8 and 21:6. He is “the Root and the Offspring of David” (verse 16), both the source of David's line and its promised heir, fulfilling Isaiah 11:1, and he is the bright Morning Star who announces the day. The one who says, “Behold, I am coming soon” is the same Jesus who was crucified and rose bodily from the dead, and his coming is the hope the whole Bible has been moving toward. The tree of life that humanity was barred from in Genesis 3 is opened by the Lamb, and the invitation is left open to every reader: “let the one who is thirsty come.”

hard.q: Jesus said he was coming soon. Why, nearly two thousand years later, hasn't he returned?
hard.a:
Christians have faced this question from the start; 2 Peter 3 addresses scoffers who asked it in the first century. Several answers are given. Preterist readers point out that much of Revelation concerns events that did come soon for the first readers, such as the judgment on the persecuting powers of their day, while the final return still lies ahead. Many others understand soon as describing the character of the present age rather than a measured interval: since Christ's resurrection, history has entered its last stage, and his coming could happen at any time, so every generation must live ready. 2 Peter 3:8-9 adds that God's time is not ours and that his apparent delay is patience, giving time for repentance. Jesus himself said that no one knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36).

These answers are held across the preterist, historicist, futurist, and idealist approaches, which differ on how much of the book is already fulfilled. The chapter's own emphasis is not on calculating the time but on readiness: keeping the words of the prophecy, washing one's robes, and praying, as the church has since its first days, “Come, Lord Jesus.”

questions: The Bible ends with the tree of life that was closed off in Genesis 3 now open. What does it mean to you that the whole story ends with healing rather than simply with escape?
The invitation is to “the one who is thirsty.” What thirst do you bring to God, and what keeps you from coming to drink freely?
Would you honestly pray “Come, Lord Jesus” today? What would have to change for that prayer to be your deepest desire?
